name: Botrytis (gray mold)
summary: A wet-weather fruit and flower rot that often shows up in strawberry and caneberry harvest talk — a disease framework, not a residue or quality score.
what_is_it: Botrytis cinerea (gray mold) infects flowers and ripening fruit, especially in cool, wet, or dense canopies. It is one of the reasons strawberry bloom sprays, caneberry canopy air-flow, and postharvest cold chain are discussed together. It is not the same organism as soil Phytophthora, and it is not a proof of poor 'food safety culture' by itself.
why_it_matters: Competitive talk about packout, bloom sprays, tunnel rain-cover, or 'wet harvest losses' is often a Botrytis story. Resistance to fungicide groups is why current regional IPM guides exist and why this page must not freeze a product list.
how_evaluated: Field incidence on flowers and fruit, postharvest rot after a defined hold, and which labeled products were used that season. A photo of fuzzy gray fruit is a teaching image, not a diagnosis of a named farm.
what_affects_it: Bloom weather, canopy density, harvest interval, wounding, and cold-chain breaks. Protected culture that keeps rain off fruit can reduce pressure and can also change other pests.
how_to_interpret: Do not treat a news mention of 'mold' as Botrytis, and do not treat this page as a spray program. Pair with IPM and with harvest methods. A variety described as 'Botrytis tolerant' is a breeder or trial claim until a scoped Fact says so.

berry_notes.note: Strawberry gray mold is classically a bloom-to-harvest disease; plasticulture and tunnels change canopy wetness, not the pathogen.
Caneberry gray mold tracks dense floricane canopies and wet harvests; trellis and air flow are cultural levers inside IPM.
Same caneberry pattern as raspberry; trailing types in wet climates are the usual extension examples, not a universal blackberry law.
